topics.title: The Psychology of People Who Would Rather Fix Than Replace
topics.safe_title: The Psychology of People Who Would Rather Fix Than Replace
topics.angle: Everyone tells you to just buy a new one, and you are on the garage floor with a wrench anyway. Open every chapter fully, each with a concrete object and a story: the IKEA effect, we value what our own hands made (Norton, Mochon and Ariely 2012); the endowment effect, the mug study (Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler 1990); why things stopped being repairable: the Phoebus light bulb cartel of 1924 that fixed bulbs at about 1000 hours, General Motors and the yearly model change under Alfred Sloan, Brooks Stevens and the phrase planned obsolescence in 1954, glued batteries; self-efficacy, a repair is a small proof that you can (Bandura 1977); Matthew Crawford and Shop Class as Soulcraft (2009); kintsugi and the Japanese word mottainai as respect for the object, told as craft and thrift with no religion; Martine Postma and the first Repair Cafe in Amsterdam in 2009; Irv Gordon and his 1966 Volvo P1800 past 3 million miles with the Guinness record; the EU right to repair rules of 2024. Then the honest catch: fixing can become sunk cost, some repairs are not safe to do yourself (brakes, airbags, gas, mains electricity), and give a plain three-question test for fix or replace with worked cash numbers. All money examples in cash, no loans, no interest, no leasing.
topics.hedge: The IKEA effect was measured in short lab tasks, so the jump to a lifetime habit is an inference.
topics.demand: proven: biggest identity outlier of the car niche
topics.why: Biggest outlier in the niche; dignified identity for the 35-plus viewer.

topics.title: Why Men Who Pay Cash for Their Car Think Differently
topics.safe_title: The Psychology of People Who Pay Cash for Their Car
topics.angle: He walks into the dealership with the number already decided and leaves without signing a single monthly payment. Chapters, each with a concrete scene: the pain of paying (Prelec and Loewenstein 1998), cash hurts a little and that is the point; Prelec and Simester 2001, MIT students paid up to about double for Celtics tickets with a card; Knutson and colleagues 2007, the brain's insula reacts to a high price; Thomas Stanley and William Danko, The Millionaire Next Door 1996, most millionaires they studied bought used and never paid top price; hedonic adaptation, the new-car smell fades in weeks (Brickman, Coates and Janoff-Bulman 1978); depreciation, a new car loses a large share of its value in the first years; the freedom of owning outright, nobody can take it back. Then the honest catch: cash can become stubbornness when a safer car is needed, and hoarding is not the goal. Exit: a plain test before any car purchase. All money examples in cash, no loans, no interest, no leasing promoted. Men only in close scenes; any woman in long loose clothing.

topics.title: Kept the Old Car vs Upgraded: 20 Years Later
topics.safe_title: Keeping an Old Car vs Upgrading: The Psychology and the Math
topics.angle: Two brothers, same salary: one upgrades every 3 years, one keeps his car. Hedonic adaptation (Brickman 1978 — careful, use Frederick & Loewenstein 1999), depreciation, positional goods (Frank). Exit: the upgrade test. Open every step of the 20 years with real depreciation maths in plain cash terms (no loans as advice), maintenance reality, the moment the old car 'wins', the moment it loses. Two brothers in scenes across year 1, 3, 7, 12, 20. Honest twist: the upgrader's joy was real but lasted about a season.
topics.demand: proven: 'Upgrading vs. Kept Old Car — 20 Years Later' [The Gen X Way] 800k (x727)
topics.why: Top outlier of the niche; story format with a payoff at the end.

topics.title: Still Driving Manual Says a Lot About You
topics.safe_title: The Psychology of People Who Still Drive Manual
topics.angle: Left foot down, right hand on the knob, he feels the engine before he hears it. Chapters: flow, the state where skill meets challenge (Csikszentmihalyi 1990); sense of agency, why doing it yourself feels like control; Cox and colleagues 2006, young drivers with attention problems drove more attentively with a manual gearbox; the cars that stopped offering a clutch, and the anti-theft joke that many thieves cannot drive stick; Europe versus America, where manual became rare; learning from a father in an empty parking lot as a rite of passage; craftsmanship and the joy of a skill that machines took away. Honest catch: automatics are now often more efficient and easier in traffic; the point is the person, not the gearbox. Exit: three signs you are a manual person even if you drive an automatic. All money examples in cash, no loans, no interest, no leasing promoted. Men only in close scenes; any woman in long loose clothing.
topics.hedge: Personality claims are pop psychology: one hedge.
topics.demand: proven: 'Still Driving Manual In A World Of Automatics Says A Lot About You' [The Gen X Way] 239k
topics.why: Proven, warm identity topic.

topics.title: Why Some Men Buy a 20-Year-Old Mercedes Instead of a New Car
topics.safe_title: The Psychology of People Who Drive Old Luxury Cars
topics.angle: A 1990s Mercedes E-Class (W124) with 400,000 km, doors that close like a bank vault. Chapters: depreciation turns yesterday's luxury into today's bargain, the buyer lets the first owner pay for the drop; the W124 and W123 as taxis from Morocco to Germany for decades; the 1989 Lexus LS400 balance test with a pyramid of glasses on the bonnet (call them water glasses, never say what was in them); quality you can feel, the thunk of the door, a sound engineered on purpose; nostalgia as a resource (Wildschut and Sedikides 2006); Veblen 1899 in reverse: the owner wants quality, not to be seen; the old luxury car as a test of skill and patience. Honest catch: parts and repairs can cost more than the car; know the weak spots before buying. Exit: a cash checklist for buying an old luxury car. All money examples in cash, no loans, no interest, no leasing promoted. Men only in close scenes; any woman in long loose clothing.

topics.title: The Psychology of People Who Know Every Car on the Road
topics.safe_title: Why Some People Can Name Every Car They See
topics.angle: A taillight glows two hundred metres away at night and he says the model and the year. Chapters: Gauthier and colleagues 2000, car experts use the same brain area for cars that everyone uses for faces (fusiform face area); chunking, Chase and Simon 1973 chess masters, experts see patterns, not pieces; childhood imprint, the boy with car cards and a catalogue; deliberate practice and the 10,000-hour idea with its honest limits (Ericsson 1993); collecting and sorting as a human drive; car spotting as a quiet way men connect, fathers and sons naming cars on a long trip. Honest catch: expertise in one field does not make you an expert everywhere. Exit: why this skill matters more than people think. All money examples in cash, no loans, no interest, no leasing promoted. Men only in close scenes; any woman in long loose clothing.

topics.title: Why Rich People Suddenly Stopped Wearing Logos and Bought Plain Sneakers
topics.safe_title: Why Rich People Suddenly Love Plain Sneakers
topics.angle: Why the very rich now wear New Balance, Onitsuka Tiger, plain Uniqlo tees while logos moved to the middle. Open fully: Veblen 1899 conspicuous consumption; Han, Nunes and Dreze 2010 'Signaling status with luxury goods' (quiet vs loud brands, patricians vs parvenus; bags with small logos cost more); Berger and Ward 2010 'Subtle signals' (insiders read small cues); Bellezza, Gino and Keinan 2014 'The Red Sneakers Effect' (nonconformity reads as status); Simmel 1904 fashion cycle; real brand stories: New Balance dad-shoe rebirth, Onitsuka Tiger's scarcity, Uniqlo basics. Five buyer types. Twist: quiet luxury is louder than logos if you can read it. Exit: three questions before buying anything: who is this for, what am I signalling, would I buy it if nobody saw it.
topics.hedge: Sales reasons mix with fashion, so psychology is only part of the story.

topics.title: Why You REALLY Chose Toyota (And Never Looked Back)
topics.safe_title: The Psychology of People Who Only Drive Toyota
topics.angle: The odometer passes 300,000 km and he simply changes the oil. Chapters: loss aversion, losing hurts about twice as much as winning feels good (Kahneman and Tversky 1979), so a reliable car is a promise that nothing bad will happen; regret aversion and the old saying nobody got fired for buying IBM; the Toyota Production System, Taiichi Ohno, the andon cord any worker can pull to stop the line, kaizen; the Hilux that a TV show tried and failed to kill in 2003 (dropped, flooded, set on fire, a building brought down on it, it still started); the Land Cruiser in deserts and aid convoys; quiet status, the choice of people who do not need to prove anything; the 1989 Lexus launch as Toyota's answer to German luxury. Honest catch: Toyota had its own big recall (2009-2011 pedals), reliability is not perfection. Exit: five types of Toyota owners. All money examples in cash, no loans, no interest, no leasing promoted. Men only in close scenes; any woman in long loose clothing.
topics.hedge: Most of these are correlational studies or stories; say honestly where the link to car choice is an inference.

topics.title: Why Men Suddenly Want a Pickup Truck After 40
topics.safe_title: The Psychology of Men Who Buy a Pickup Truck After 40
topics.angle: He has never towed anything and the truck is already in his head. Chapters: the U-shaped curve of life satisfaction, lowest around the late forties (Blanchflower and Oswald 2008); Elliott Jaques named the midlife crisis in 1965, and what it really is; generativity, Erik Erikson's need to be useful and to build (1950); the Ford F-Series, America's best-selling vehicle for decades; competence and usefulness as identity, the truck as a promise that he can still carry things for people; the Toyota Hilux and small kei trucks around the world as work tools; honest catch: many buyers rarely use the bed, and a truck will not solve what a conversation could. Exit: three healthy ways to use that midlife pull. All money examples in cash, no loans, no interest, no leasing promoted. Men only in close scenes; any woman in long loose clothing.

diagnosis_2026-10-26:
Own channel: 9 subs, median 109 views. The only real outlier is 'Why You REALLY Chose BMW, Mercedes, or Audi' (x4.6, 9.9 min): brand names the viewer already owns or wants + 'really' (hidden reason). Grey-car 'types' (x1.9) is the second hit, so the car-psychology line works; the off-niche 'Why He Stopped Posting' (x0.3) flopped and the debt-flavoured 'cars they can't afford' underperformed (x0.7).
Niche demand: 'The Psychology of People Who ...' about one concrete car habit is a proven machine (Nous Psychology: 620k know how to work on cars, 407k modify their cars, 115k keep cars spotless; 'Driving the same car for 10 years says a lot about you' 734k). Viewer question behind all of them: 'what does my habit/choice say about me?'.
Brand psychology has huge outliers when it names famous brands and exposes the hidden mechanism: 'How Apple and Nike have branded your brain' 4.9M, 'How luxury brands brainwash you to buy' 3.9M, 'The psychology of premium branding' 1.4M, 'Pricing psychology explained' 225k. 'The hidden psychology behind a car's face' (116k) joins both lines.
Length: winners sit at 8-12 min; our best was 9.9 min, so 10-12 min is the target, not 15.
Gaps: car-face design, keeping one car for years, white cars (colour series started with red and grey), quiet luxury logos, why rich people drive boring cars, pricing tricks, supermarket layout, car modifying. Title pattern to keep: 'Why You REALLY…', 'The Psychology of People Who…', a concrete object + a hidden reason.
